context_blurb:
Step into a forest and look around. Trees, birds, beetles and mushrooms live there. So do things that were never alive: rocks, soil, water, air and sunlight. Every part acts on the others, and each living thing depends on the rest. Knowing how the parts fit together shows us what keeps a place healthy, and how people can harm it or help it.

All the living things in a place, together with the nonliving things around them, make up an ecosystem, with every part acting on the others. Ecosystems come in all sizes. At low tide, the sea leaves small pools in the rocks along the shore. Peer into one and you find a complete tiny ecosystem: snails, crabs, seaweed and small fish, with seawater, stone and sunshine.

Scientists sort an ecosystem's parts into two groups. An ecosystem's living parts, its plants, animals, fungi and bacteria, are called its biotic factors. Pine trees, deer and even the bacteria in soil are all biotic factors. An ecosystem's nonliving parts, such as sunlight, water, air, soil, rock and temperature, are its abiotic factors.

Living things need the nonliving parts as much as they need each other. Visit a pond on a cool, sunny morning, and you may see turtles lined up on the rocks. A turtle gets its body heat mostly from its surroundings, so it climbs out to soak up the warmth. A turtle warming itself on a sunny rock is using two abiotic factors at once: the sunlight and the stone. A hawk catching a mouse is using a biotic factor instead: another living thing.

Every living thing also needs a habitat. A habitat is the place where a living thing makes its home and finds everything it needs: food, water, shelter and space. A forest gives its deer and owls all of these: food, streams, thick brush to hide in and room to wander. So the forest is their habitat. A den or a nest gives shelter, but shelter is only one part of a habitat.

A healthy ecosystem usually holds many different kinds of living things, and scientists call that variety biodiversity. An ecosystem with many kinds of living things usually stands up better to trouble, such as a drought or a disease. Once, a disease killed most of the chestnut trees in some great forests. The forests lived on, because plenty of other kinds of trees grew there as well. Predators belong in a healthy ecosystem, too. Take them away, and a whole food web can be thrown out of balance.

People can harm an ecosystem or help it. Tree roots grip the soil and bind it together. Clear every tree off a steep hill, and that grip is lost. With the trees gone, no roots hold the soil together, so heavy rain washes it down the slope. After a storm, the streams below run brown with mud.

Pollution can harm a lake in a sneaky way. Farmers spread fertilizer to help their crops grow, but rain can wash it off the fields and into a lake. There the fertilizer feeds algae, tiny green living things that grow in water. The algae spread so fast that the lake turns green. When the algae die, bacteria break them down and use up the oxygen in the water. Fish need that oxygen to breathe, so when it runs low, many of them die. The green colour is not what kills them; the missing oxygen is.

People can help a lake too. One of the best ways is planting shrubs and tall grasses along the shore. This strip of wild plants catches soil and fertilizer before the rain can wash them into the lake, and its deep roots hold the bank in place. A mowed lawn cannot do this job, because its grass roots reach down only a few centimetres.
